title: What Is a Good Indoor Air Quality Level?
h1: What Is a Good Indoor Air Quality Level for Your Home?
description: Good indoor air means low fine particles, CO2 under about 1,000 ppm, humidity of 30 to 50 percent and low VOCs. Learn what the numbers mean for your home.
quick_answer: Good indoor air quality usually means fine particle levels (PM2.5) at or below about 9 micrograms per cubic meter, carbon dioxide under about 1,000 ppm, relative humidity between about 30 and 50 percent, and low levels of VOCs from cleaners and new furnishings. There isn't one official score for homes, so it helps to look at each measurement separately.
body:
Indoor air quality monitors have become common, and many of them show a long list of numbers. It's easy to see a reading and not know whether it's fine or a problem. Here's what the main measurements mean and what levels are generally considered good.

What do the main measurements mean?

MeasurementWhat it isGenerally good level
PM2.5Fine particles from smoke, cooking, dust and outdoor pollution9 µg/m³ or less
CO2Carbon dioxide from people breathing, a sign of ventilationUnder about 1,000 ppm
Relative humidityMoisture in the airAbout 30 to 50 percent
VOCsGases from cleaners, paints, furniture and cookingAs low as possible
Carbon monoxideA poisonous gas from fuel-burning appliancesNone detected

What PM2.5 level is good indoors?

PM2.5 means particles 2.5 microns or smaller. They're small enough to get deep into the lungs. The EPA's Air Quality Index rates a 24-hour PM2.5 average of 9 µg/m³ or less as "good." Indoors, a sensible target is to stay at or below that level most of the time.

Cooking, candles, vacuuming and wildfire smoke can spike PM2.5 quickly. Short spikes while cooking are normal. Readings that stay high for hours point to a filtration problem or an ongoing source.

What CO2 level is good?

Outdoor air usually sits around 400 to 450 ppm. Indoors, CO2 rises as people breathe, especially in closed bedrooms and offices. Levels under about 1,000 ppm are widely used as a sign of decent ventilation. Readings well above that often mean the room needs more fresh air.

CO2 isn't usually harmful at typical home levels, but high CO2 can come with stuffiness and drowsiness, and it signals that other pollutants may be building up too.

What humidity is best?

The EPA recommends keeping indoor humidity between about 30 and 50 percent, and below 60 percent to limit mold and dust mites. Coastal homes in Southern California can run on the humid side, especially in cooler months. Inland homes can get very dry during Santa Ana winds, which can irritate skin, eyes and sinuses.

A dehumidifier helps in damp homes. A whole-house humidifier can help in dry ones.

What about VOCs and carbon monoxide?

VOCs, or volatile organic compounds, come from cleaning products, air fresheners, paint, new furniture, flooring and cooking. Consumer monitors measure them differently, so watch for changes rather than exact numbers. Spikes after cleaning or painting are common. Ventilating during and after those activities helps.

Carbon monoxide should not be present at all. Every home with gas appliances, a fireplace or an attached garage should have working CO alarms. If a CO alarm sounds, get everyone out and call 911.

How often should I check my readings?

A monitor is most useful when you watch patterns over a few weeks. Notice when readings rise, such as during cooking, after cleaning, overnight in bedrooms or when the AC hasn't run for a while. Those patterns point to the source and the fix. A single high reading on its own is rarely a cause for worry.

If readings stay high even after you have changed the filter and ventilated, have a technician look at the system. Leaky ducts, a dirty coil or an undersized filter can all keep numbers up.

How can I improve my indoor air quality?

  1. Upgrade filtration. A higher-rated HVAC filter or a whole-house media filter cuts particles throughout the home.
  2. Ventilate. Use kitchen and bath exhaust fans, and open windows when outdoor air is clean.
  3. Control humidity. Keep it in the 30 to 50 percent range.
  4. Seal duct leaks. Leaky return ducts can pull dusty attic or garage air into the system.
  5. Reduce sources. Choose low-VOC products and avoid burning candles and incense often.
  6. Plan for smoke. During wildfire smoke, keep windows closed, run filtration and use portable HEPA purifiers in bedrooms.

Our indoor air quality team can recommend filtration, purifiers, humidity control and ventilation options that match what your readings show.
faqs: Is there an official indoor air quality score for homes?
No single official score applies to homes. Monitors often combine readings into their own index. It's more useful to look at PM2.5, CO2, humidity and VOCs individually.
Are home air quality monitors accurate?
They're good for spotting trends and spikes, like smoke or cooking. Readings vary between brands, especially for VOCs, so use them as a guide rather than an exact measurement.
Why is my CO2 high in the bedroom at night?
A closed door and people breathing for hours raise CO2. Cracking a window, leaving the door ajar or improving ventilation can help bring it down.
What humidity is too high indoors?
Readings that stay above 60 percent raise the risk of mold, dust mites and musty smells. Running exhaust fans, the AC or a dehumidifier can help bring humidity down.
